# JSON-LD binding {#sec-binding-json-ld}

[Normative]{.status}

## Overview

The JSON-LD binding carries framework information over the internet and other IP networks:
between vessels and their shadows, between shore services, and on board wherever IP is available.
It is the only binding expected to carry information at **full fidelity**.

This binding covers JSON-LD on every transport that carries it:

HTTP
: The baseline transport.

CoAP
: An alternative transport for constrained devices and links, including group communication over IP multicast.

## Transport mechanics

The working proposal (see [decision record 0003](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0003-things-as-web-resources.md)):

- Every Thing is a **web resource**, identified by its IRI.
- **HTTP** [@rfc9110] is the baseline protocol, using its standard methods.

### Change notifications {#sec-change-notifications}

A change notification tells a participant that a Thing has changed (@sec-changes), so that it can fetch the Thing if it is interested.
A notification carries the kind of change, create, update or delete, and a link to the Thing.
It may also carry hints, so that a receiver can decide whether to fetch the Thing without fetching it: the IRI of the new version (@sec-versions), the Thing's type, when it was modified, and its area as a bounding box.
A receiver that already holds the version a notification names need not fetch it.
A notification is not the Thing, and a receiver acts on the Thing it fetches.

::: {.requirement #ncf-bnd-jsonld-003}
**NCF-BND-JSONLD-003** · *Draft*\
A change notification MUST state the kind of change and link to the Thing that changed.
:::

For a delete there is nothing to fetch.
Since a forged notification of a delete could suppress a warning, a receiver acts on one without confirming it only when it trusts the channel that carried it, such as a TLS connection to the Thing's origin (@sec-origins).
Otherwise it confirms the delete by retrieving the Thing.

::: {.requirement #ncf-bnd-jsonld-004}
**NCF-BND-JSONLD-004** · *Draft*\
A receiver MUST NOT act on a notification of a delete without retrieving the Thing, unless it trusts the channel that carried the notification.
:::

The link is a locator: it need only lead to the Thing, and may be made for the receiver, for example from the address through which the receiver connected.
The receiver identifies the Thing by the IRI its representation gives itself ([NCF-SEM-004](../overview/semantic-model.qmd#ncf-sem-004), [NCF-SEM-043](../overview/semantic-model.qmd#ncf-sem-043)).

A receiver that may have missed notifications, for example after reconnecting, fetches again the Things it holds, with conditional requests so that a Thing that has not changed costs little.
A transport may also offer a point from which to resume, such as the `id` of a server-sent event with `Last-Event-ID` [@whatwg-html], or an MQTT persistent session [@mqtt5]; offering one is optional.

CoAP Observe is the exception: each notification is the resource's representation itself [@rfc7641], not a link to it.

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
How is a change notification encoded: which properties name the kind of change, the link and each hint, and is a notification itself JSON-LD?
:::

### Requesting changes {#sec-requesting-changes}

Any participant can request a change to a Thing, with `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` [@rfc5789] or `DELETE`.
A request is not a change.
Only the Thing's origin applies changes ([NCF-SEM-031](../overview/semantic-model.qmd#ncf-sem-031)): it decides, under its owner's authorization policy (@sec-identity-authorization), whether to make the change, and the owner makes it, and may sign it (@sec-trust-security).
A change made on request is the owner's change, and the requester appears in its provenance (@sec-provenance).
An origin can accept a request before the owner has made the change, for example when the owner must review or sign it.

::: {.requirement #ncf-bnd-jsonld-005}
**NCF-BND-JSONLD-005** · *Draft*\
A server MUST NOT apply a request to change a Thing unless the Thing's owner authorizes the change.
:::

When a participant requests the creation of a Thing in another's collection, such as a sighting reported to an agency, who owns the Thing that results depends on the collection owner's contribution policy.
Either ownership passes to the collection's owner, as with a work made for hire, or the contributor keeps it and licenses the Thing to the collection's owner.
Either way, the Thing that results states its owner and its terms (@sec-rights), and the contributor appears in its provenance.

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
How does a collection's owner publish its contribution policy, so that a contributor knows it before contributing?
Where the contributor keeps ownership, which origin applies later changes to the Thing?
:::

### HTTP

See [provisional decision 0009](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0009-json-ld-over-http.md).

::: {.callout-note title="HTTP versions"}
HTTP/1.1 [@rfc9112] is the baseline version; a server can also offer HTTP/2 [@rfc9113] or HTTP/3 [@rfc9114] ([NCF-BND-JSONLD-001](#ncf-bnd-jsonld-001)).
A client can find which versions a server supports from the `alpn` parameter of the server's DNS HTTPS resource record [@rfc9460].
:::

#### Getting current state

Retrieve the resource at the Thing's IRI with `GET`.

A Thing that has ended, such as a withdrawn or expired notice, is returned like any other, with `200 OK` and its status in its representation ([NCF-VOC-NOT-001](../vocab/notices.qmd#ncf-voc-not-001)).
A deleted Thing is answered with `410 Gone` [@rfc9110].

::: {.requirement #ncf-bnd-jsonld-009}
**NCF-BND-JSONLD-009** · *Draft*\
A server SHOULD answer a request for a Thing that has been deleted with `410 Gone`.
:::

#### Requesting changes

Request a change with `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` [@rfc5789] or `DELETE`; the Thing's origin decides whether to make it (@sec-requesting-changes).

#### Receiving changes

A participant learns of changes by one of:

Polling
: Repeating `GET` on the resource.

Server-sent events
: A stream of change notifications from the server over HTTP [@whatwg-html].

WebSocket
: A two-way connection [@rfc6455], for a participant that both sends and receives.

MQTT
: The server refers the participant to an MQTT broker [@mqtt5] and a topic on which changes are published.

#### Addressing and routing

A Thing is addressed by its IRI.

An MQTT broker is addressed by an `mqtt:` or `mqtts:` URI.
These schemes are provisionally registered with IANA and identify only the broker, not a topic.
This binding extends them so that the path gives the topic, for example `mqtts://broker.example.org/vessels/1/sightings`.

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Is the topic given in the URI path, as above, or in a separate property alongside a broker-only URI, as in the W3C Web of Things MQTT binding?
If in the path, how are the MQTT wildcards `+` and `#` encoded, given that `#` begins a URI fragment?
:::

#### Constraints

::: {.callout-warning title="To be written"}
Operation over intermittent, metered and high-latency links (for example satellite).
:::

### CoAP

See [provisional decision 0010](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0010-coap-transport.md).

CoAP [@rfc7252] is a web transfer protocol for constrained devices and networks, carried over UDP.

#### Getting current state

Retrieve the resource with `GET`.

#### Requesting changes

Request a change with a mutating method such as `POST`, `PUT` or `DELETE`; the Thing's origin decides whether to make it (@sec-requesting-changes).

#### Receiving changes

A participant learns of changes by one of:

Polling
: Repeating `GET` on the resource.

Observe
: The participant registers with the server and receives a notification each time the resource changes [@rfc7641].

Group communication
: The server sends changes to an IP multicast group, as specified in `draft-ietf-core-groupcomm-bis`.

#### Addressing and routing

A Thing is addressed by a `coap:` or `coaps:` URI.
A multicast group is addressed by a group URI: a `coap:` URI whose host is the group's IP multicast address, for example `coap://[ff02::fd]/sightings`.

::: {.callout-note title="Group communication specification"}
`draft-ietf-core-groupcomm-bis` replaces RFC 7390 [@rfc7390], the Experimental specification of CoAP group communication, and will obsolete it when published.
It is intended as a Proposed Standard, but is still an Internet-Draft and may change before publication.
:::

#### Constraints

::: {.callout-warning title="To be written"}
Message size: a JSON-LD Thing with a persistent signature may not fit in one UDP datagram (see the compact forms to be written under Representation).
Link-local multicast does not leave the network it is sent on, so group communication is limited to the vessel's own network.
:::

## Representation

JSON-LD [@json-ld11] is the basic representation of Things.

A payload is JSON.
Its JSON-LD context is given in one of two ways:

- an `@context` property in the document, served as `application/ld+json`; or
- over HTTP, a `Link` header with the relation `http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld#context`, with the document served as `application/json`.

The JSON-LD representation of a Thing links to each mechanism for receiving changes other than polling, with the link relation type `monitor` [@rfc5989; @rfc8288] ([NCF-BND-JSONLD-002](#ncf-bnd-jsonld-002)).
The target URI identifies the mechanism: an `https:` URI for server-sent events, a `wss:` URI for a WebSocket, an `mqtts:` URI for an MQTT broker and topic, a `coaps:` URI for CoAP Observe, or a `coap:` group URI for CoAP group communication.
RFC 5989 defines `monitor` links to SIP URIs and leaves other URI schemes to other specifications; this binding defines them for these schemes.

In a JSON-LD document, a `monitor` link is a property named by the IANA relation IRI `http://www.iana.org/assignments/relation/monitor`.

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Is the IANA relation IRI a stable identifier for this use?
RFC 5988 [@rfc5988] described this form of relation IRI, but RFC 8288, which replaced it, does not.
If it is not stable, a term in a framework vocabulary is used instead.
:::

### Versions and caching

A Thing's representation states the IRI of the version it carries (@sec-versions).
The entity tag of a response [@rfc9110] is the server's own, and a server can derive it from the version's IRI; a strong entity tag differs between representations of the same version, such as JSON-LD and CBOR-LD.

A receiver revalidates a cached representation with a conditional `GET` and `If-None-Match`.
A request to change a Thing is made conditional on the version it was based on with `If-Match`, so that the origin refuses it with `412 Precondition Failed` if the Thing has changed since.

::: {.requirement #ncf-bnd-jsonld-006}
**NCF-BND-JSONLD-006** · *Draft*\
A request to change a Thing SHOULD be conditional, with `If-Match`, on the version of the Thing it was based on.
:::

A response links the version it carries to others with `Link` headers [@rfc8288] and the version relations [@rfc5829]: `latest-version` to the current version, and `predecessor-version` to each version it succeeds.
An earlier version that its owner keeps is served at the version's own IRI.

A cache does not keep a representation beyond the Thing's next scheduled change (@sec-changes), since the Thing may be a different version from then on.

::: {.requirement #ncf-bnd-jsonld-007}
**NCF-BND-JSONLD-007** · *Draft*\
A server SHOULD set the freshness lifetime of a representation, with `Cache-Control: max-age` or `Expires` [@rfc9111], to end no later than the time of the Thing's next scheduled change.
:::

### Contexts

A Data Integrity proof is verified over the RDF a representation expresses, which depends on its JSON-LD context (@sec-trust-security).
A context that could change at its IRI would let anyone who controls it change what a signed Thing means without breaking its signature.
A context used by a signed Thing therefore never changes at its IRI: a changed context is published at a new IRI, and a receiver can cache a context indefinitely.

::: {.requirement #ncf-bnd-jsonld-008}
**NCF-BND-JSONLD-008** · *Draft*\
A JSON-LD context used by a persistently signed Thing MUST NOT change at its IRI; a changed context MUST be published at a new IRI.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
How does a receiver check that a context it retrieves is the one a signer used, for example by a digest of the context?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="To be written"}
JSON-LD contexts for each vocabulary module; content negotiation; compact forms for constrained links.
:::

## Fidelity

All Things can be carried without loss.

## Trust

- Transport security: TLS for HTTP, with servers identified by WebPKI certificates; DTLS for `coaps:` [@rfc7252].
- Client identity: OpenID Connect; authorization: OAuth 2.0 (@sec-trust-security).
- Persistent signatures: Data Integrity proofs over the canonical RDF dataset of the Thing's version, embedded in the JSON-LD representation ([NCF-TRU-002](../overview/trust-security.qmd#ncf-tru-002)).

OSCORE [@rfc8613] can protect CoAP messages end to end, including through proxies.
Like TLS and DTLS, it protects a message in transit, not the Thing after it is received, so it does not replace a persistent signature.
Group OSCORE, an Internet-Draft (`draft-ietf-core-oscore-groupcomm`), would extend this protection to group communication.
Without it, a Thing sent to a multicast group is protected only by its persistent signature.

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Is OSCORE used to protect CoAP messages, and Group OSCORE for group communication once it is published?
:::

## Requirements

::: {.requirement #ncf-bnd-jsonld-001}
**NCF-BND-JSONLD-001** · *Draft*\
A server that offers HTTP MUST allow a client to negotiate HTTP/1.1, and MAY also allow HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.
:::

::: {.requirement #ncf-bnd-jsonld-002}
**NCF-BND-JSONLD-002** · *Draft*\
The JSON-LD representation of a Thing SHOULD include a `monitor` link for each mechanism, other than polling, by which changes to the Thing can be received.
:::

## Examples

Examples of an organism, a sighting and a notice as JSON-LD are in @sec-examples.
